title: Q&A with Climate Scientist David Victor, Part 2: AI Data Centers and Resources | Dimensional
gist: Climate scientist David Victor argues AI data centers are approaching 5% of US power demand and are defaulting to natural gas because speed, not cleanliness, wins the 'first to power' race, while speculative grid interconnection requests, hyped small modular reactor deals, and water-scarcity fears are largely distractions from the real story: a US-China gap in power access that is turning electricity into a strategic asset for the AI race.

themes.theme: Data center power demand and the gas default

insights.claim: Data centers are racing on a 'first to power' business model, choosing natural gas as their default power source because it is the cheapest and fastest option in most of the US, not because it is cleanest.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Expect continued gas demand growth and gas turbine capex tied to data center buildout, favoring gas infrastructure and equipment names over a pure renewables-led power story in the near term.
insights.quote: these companies are in an arms race with each other to get their AI into a variety of applications
insights.locator: An interesting feature is that data centers want power fast

insights.claim: US data center electricity demand is approaching 5% of total US power demand and rising very steeply.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of the AI-driven load addition for utility capacity planning and power-demand forecasting models.
insights.quote: it's approaching 5% of total power demand and rising very steeply
insights.locator: Data centers are certainly a big source of growth

insights.claim: Victor pushes back on the narrative that data centers are driving the entirety of US emissions growth, calling it 'hyperventilation' since data centers account for roughly 4-5% of total US emissions, comparable to the airline industry.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Investors modeling ESG/carbon risk should size the data center emissions contribution against a like-for-like sector (airlines) rather than treating it as the dominant driver of the 2025 US emissions uptick.
insights.quote: the idea that data centers will cause all the growth in emissions is, to me, a degree of hyperventilation
insights.locator: Is the increase in energy demand from data centers high enough

themes.theme: Small modular reactors: hype outrunning delivery

insights.claim: Numerous data center companies have signed MOUs for small modular reactor (SMR) nuclear power, but Victor characterizes these deals as 'just press releases' with no operating projects yet, because data centers cannot wait for first-of-a-kind energy projects.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Temper near-term SMR-driven demand theses for nuclear equipment and uranium; the MOU pipeline is not yet a revenue or construction pipeline.
insights.quote: We've seen a number of data center companies sign memorandums of understanding for small modular reactors—these would be novel nuclear energy supply projects. But so far those are just press releases.
insights.locator: We've seen a number of data center companies sign memorandums of understanding

insights.claim: Once SMRs become truly available and reliable with known costs, Victor expects data centers to become eager buyers of that power.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: The catalyst to watch for real SMR procurement is cost certainty plus proven reliability, not MOU announcements; that milestone, not press releases, should trigger re-rating of SMR-linked equities.
insights.locator: When small reactors become truly available and reliable

themes.theme: Grid planning breakdown and interconnection reform

insights.claim: Almost all data center interconnection requests filed with grid operators are speculative and may never materialize into actual power draw, making grid capacity planning extremely difficult compared to five years ago.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Utility and grid capex plans built on current interconnection queues likely overstate real future load; watch for queue reforms (filing fees, escrow requirements) as a leading indicator of which projects are real.
insights.quote: almost all interconnection requests are totally speculative, and they may or may not end up needing the power they had requested
insights.locator: Can you expand on how it has started to transform the grid?

insights.claim: Reforms such as higher filing fees and escrow requirements to screen speculative interconnection requests are underway across the grid but are taking time to implement.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Track state/regional grid-reform timelines as a gating factor for how fast data center power capacity can actually be brought online.
insights.locator: Those reforms are underway in many parts of the grid

insights.claim: If large loads like data centers become responsive to grid conditions, they could lower overall electricity costs by amortizing the grid's fixed capital cost over much higher throughput, but Victor notes this 'hope and promise' has not yet materialized because it requires a highly responsive grid that does not yet exist.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: A bull case for falling electricity prices exists but is conditional on demand-response infrastructure and utility rate design catching up; not yet investable as a realized trend.
insights.quote: these new power loads are taking a very expensive capital asset, which is the grid, and amortizing that asset over a much larger throughput of electricity
insights.locator: In theory, data centers could be a boon to political forces

insights.claim: Who pays for new grid infrastructure driven by data center interconnection is a live political question, arriving at a time when US electricity prices are already broadly rising and affordability is a top political concern.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Electricity affordability is becoming a political flashpoint; expect rate-case and regulatory friction risk for utilities serving large data center loads.
insights.locator: A key political question is who is going to pay for this grid infrastructure

themes.theme: Demand flexibility and the US-China power gap

insights.claim: Data centers are sorting compute workloads into high-priority (immediate, like an on-demand AI image request) and low-priority (deferrable over a day or more) categories to shift load away from grid peak periods.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Data center demand may be more flexible than headline capacity numbers suggest, potentially reducing the need for new peaker-plant capacity if load-shifting scales.
insights.locator: Data centers want to figure out which compute requirements

insights.claim: AI companies are now pushing for other grid loads, including power-hungry industrial loads, to become more responsive as well, spreading demand-flexibility pressure beyond the data center sector itself.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Demand-response technology and services providers could see a broader addressable market as AI-driven pressure extends flexibility requirements into heavy industry.
insights.locator: we are starting to see more pressure from AI companies

insights.claim: US AI compute is largely power-constrained, while new AI-related loads in China face far fewer problems accessing power, making power access a strategic asset in the AI competition between the two countries.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: US grid build-out speed is a national AI-competitiveness variable versus China; slow US interconnection and permitting timelines are a tangible risk factor for the pace of US AI infrastructure scaling.
insights.quote: new AI-related loads in China seem to be having many fewer problems getting access to power. Up to a point, access to power has become a strategic asset for the AI revolution.
insights.locator: most AI-related compute loads are in the United States

insights.claim: Victor sees no significant water consumption issue from data centers because new large facilities typically use closed-loop cooling systems that continuously recirculate water rather than open-loop evaporative systems that consume it.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Investors should discount water-scarcity as a material ESG or cost risk factor for modern data center builds; it is not the constraint the headlines suggest.
insights.quote: the big new data centers are typically closed-loop systems that continuously recirculate the water in various ways, use the heat for various purposes, and do not consume significant amounts of water
insights.locator: Water is one of those topics that once it's in the news

insights.claim: 79% of water drawn from the Colorado River goes to agriculture, which is priced below residential and industrial rates, meaning any future water-pricing reform would primarily hit agriculture, not data centers.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Regulatory or ESG focus on data center water use is largely misplaced; agricultural water pricing reform, not data center restrictions, is the more consequential policy lever to watch in Western water markets.
insights.quote: 79% of the water drawn from the Colorado River goes to agriculture
insights.locator: Interestingly, water pricing and water allocation in the US

insights.claim: It remains an open question whether AI will ultimately favor renewable energy or fossil fuels, since the same AI capabilities that enable running complex, renewables-heavy low-emission grids also make it easier to run complex refineries and find and produce oil and coal.
insights.speaker: David Victor
insights.so_what: Do not treat AI as a one-directional clean-energy tailwind; it is a dual-use efficiency technology that also boosts fossil fuel extraction and refining, so hedge exposure across both clean and fossil energy sub-sectors rather than assuming AI purely benefits decarbonization plays.
insights.quote: There is a great race underway in which clean has a slight advantage, but it's not clear how that's going to play out.
